newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil business community in mourning after crash.
newsitem.headline: Brazil business community in mourning after crash.

text.p: Brazil's financial community was in mourning on Friday, trying to overcome the shock of a tragic air disaster that took the lives of dozens of the country's businessmen.
TAM Lineas Aereas Flight 402, which crashed into a densely populated Sao Paulo neighborhood soon after take-off on Thursday, was scheduled to carry 96 passengers and crew to Rio de Janeiro.
A majority of the passengers were businessmen, bankers and executives from top Brazilian and international companies headed to Rio for morning meetings.

"It could have been anyone of us on that plane. I have made the trip a thousand times. That is why all the financial markets were so affected by this," said an economist at a Brazilian bank who asked not to be named.
Thousands of businessmen make the routine commute each week between Brazil's two main financial centers, much like their counterparts in Los Angeles and San Francisco or New York and Washington.
Leading Brazilian retail bank Unibanco lost eight officials in various departments of the bank. The loss slowed the bank's trading operations to a quarter of normal activity on Thursday.
Coca-Cola, Citibank, Bank of Boston, Chase, Siemens, Parmalat, Hoescht, Boehringer and Asea Brown Boveri were among the multinational firms that had executives aboard Flight 402.

News of the accident froze trading on Sao Paulo and Rio de Janeiro stock markets, where traders put down their pencils and tickets to learn more about the fatal flight, which killed all 96 onboard and at least eight on the ground.
Trading volume on Sao Paulo's stock exchange on Thursday was off almost 50 percent.
"This accident stopped the market. There were many people who lost colleagues in the crash and it robbed them of any desire to work," a Sao Paulo trader said.

TAM is Latin America's fastest growing regional carrier. Ironically, the airline has attributed much of its success to building a niche among business-class clients by adapting flight times to meet the financial community's hectic schedules and offering an attractive frequent-flyer plan.
Veterans of the commute say it was the first accident between the two cities in more than 20 years.
Despite Thursday's tragedy, most in the financial community said the markets would begin to return to normal on Monday.
"Business was certainly affected by this yesterday and today. I think next week we will get back to normal," said Claudio Haddad, chief executive officer at Brazilian investment bank Garantia.
